chapter: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
title: 125th Street, Duke Yelman and the Cotton Club color line
summary: He describes 125th Street as a mosaic, a quarter-a-head club-date band as a substitute for the Cotton Club, and the Cotton Club's exclusion of Black patrons.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Furthermore, this is New York City now, and 125th Street was gradually becoming a mosaic kind of... I don't know, is that the right word...?
You mean a mosaic of different...

Yeah. And colors. Ethnic... It was predominantly... I mean, Jewish-owned, but then predominantly the buyers were Blacks and Spanish and things like that. But there was a Duke Yelman(?)... See, if you couldn't go to the Cotton Club to hear Duke Ellington, you paid a quarter and went down and heard Duke Yelman(?).
Well, Duke Yelman would be like a club date band. I mean, he was Jewish, but I mean, he was very popular, because the people that couldn't afford to go to the much-heralded, expensive Cotton Club...
Well, they wouldn't allow Black people in there unless they were famous, would they?
I mean, I heard somebody said that when Paul Robeson went there they sat him behind the cloak room or something.
